strings.title: Make the Next Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add up to the next ten first, then add what is left.
strings.keywords: next ten, friendly number, break apart, jump
strings.connection: First string of the week. Sets up the open number line and the idea that 10 ones make a ten.
watchFor: Counting on by ones (28, 29, 30, 31...): accept it, then ask "Is there a jump that gets you to a ten?"
Breaking the number the wrong way (28 + 5 as 28 + 3 + 2 = 33, but stopping at 31): ask "How much of the 5 have you used?"
Not knowing the partners of 10: keep a quick reference (8 and 2, 7 and 3...) and celebrate students who use them.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the first problems help with the later ones?" Land: get to the next ten, then add the rest.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: "8 and 2 make a ten." Ask: "How does 8 + 2 help?" Model: numberline 28 +2
Look for: 28 + 2 = 30, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did the 5 go?" Word choice: "I broke 5 into 2 and 3." Model: numberline 28 +2 +3
Look for: 48 + 2 = 50, then 4 more. Ask: "How did you know to use 2?" Model: numberline 48 +2 +4
Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 5 more. Ask: "What is the next ten after 67?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +5
Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 15 more; or 67 + 10 + 8. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +15
Look for: the same moves as 67 + 8. Ask: "Predict before I show it. What changed?" Model: numberline 167 +3 +5

strings.title: Split by Place Value
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Add tens with tens and ones with ones, then put them together. When the ones make more than 10, that makes another ten.
strings.keywords: tens, ones, hundreds, place value, partial sums, make a new ten
strings.connection: Day 1 made a ten on the number line. Today the ones combine into a new ten when we add by place value.
watchFor: Saying "3 + 4" for 30 + 40: ask "Is it 3 + 4 or 30 + 40? How do you know?" and write the real values.
Writing 713 for 70 + 13: ask "How many tens are in 13? Where do they go?"
Forgetting the ones: ask "Did you add every part?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What happened when the ones added up to more than 10?" Land: 10 ones make a new ten, and it joins the other tens.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens. Ask: "How many tens?"
Look for: a known fact, or 6 + 4 + 3. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 13?"
Look for: 70 + 13 = 83. Ask: "How did the last two problems help?" Word choice: "13 ones is 1 ten and 3 ones." Model: text 36 + 47 = 30 + 40 + 6 + 7 ; = 70 + 13 ; = 83
Look for: 70 + 14. Ask: "Where does the extra ten come from?" Model: text 28 + 56 = 20 + 50 + 8 + 6 ; = 70 + 14 ; = 84
Look for: 70 + 13, or 45 + 30 + 8 on the number line. Ask: "Did anyone do it another way?" Model: numberline 45 +30 +8
Look for: 100 + 50 + 12. Ask: "What happens to the hundreds?" Model: text 125 + 37 = 100 + 20 + 30 + 5 + 7 ; = 100 + 50 + 12 ; = 162
Look for: 400 + 70 + 13. Ask: "Which part makes a new ten?" Model: text 356 + 127 = 300 + 100 + 50 + 20 + 6 + 7 ; = 400 + 70 + 13 ; = 483

strings.title: Over the Hundred
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Get to the next hundred (or ten), then add what is left. Tens can regroup into a new hundred, just like ones regroup into a ten.
strings.keywords: next hundred, friendly number, regroup, 10 tens
strings.connection: Day 1 got to the next ten. Today we get to the next hundred.
watchFor: Writing 1003 for 95 + 8: ask "Is it more or less than 200? Where is it on the line?"
Losing track of the hundreds (186 + 25 = 111): ask "About how big should the answer be?"
Breaking the number awkwardly: accept it, then ask "Which jump would get you to a hundred?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is getting to the next hundred like getting to the next ten?" Land: 10 tens make a hundred, just like 10 ones make a ten.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens. Ask: "How many tens make 100?"
Look for: 95 + 5 = 100, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did you stop?" Model: numberline 95 +5 +3
Look for: the same as 95 + 8, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same? What changed?" Model: numberline 195 +5 +3
Look for: 186 + 14 = 200, then 11 more; or 186 + 20 + 5. Ask: "How did you know to use 14?" Model: numberline 186 +14 +11
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 5 more. Ask: "How many tens did it take to cross 300?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +5
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 13 more. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +13
Look for: 368 + 32 = 400, then 13; or 368 + 40 + 5. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?" Model: numberline 368 +32 +13

strings.title: Add a Friendly Number, Then Take Back
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: When a number is close to a friendly number (a ten or a hundred), add the friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: friendly number, close to, too much, take back
strings.connection: Days 1–3 added up to a friendly number. Today we jump past it and come back.
watchFor: Forgetting to take back (46 + 9 = 56): ask "Is 46 + 9 more or less than 46 + 10?"
Going the wrong way (46 + 9 = 57): ask the same question and show both on the line.
Taking back the wrong amount (135 + 98 = 232): ask "How far is 98 from 100?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is this a good strategy?" Land: when one number is close to a ten or a hundred.

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and land?" Model: numberline 46 +10
Look for: 46 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 46 + 10 help?" Word choice: "too much by 1, take it back." Model: numberline 46 +10 -1
Look for: 46 + 20, back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 46 + 9 and 46 + 19?" Model: numberline 46 +20 -1
Look for: 46 + 30, back 1. Ask: "Predict how someone will do it." Model: numberline 46 +30 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 1. Ask: "Why 100?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 2. Ask: "What changed from the last one?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -2
Look for: 247 + 200, back 2; or 245 + 200 (give and take). Ask: "Which friendly number did you use?" Model: numberline 247 +200 -2

strings.title: Where Does the New Ten Go?
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Connect mental strategies to the standard algorithm: the carried 1 is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens).
strings.keywords: regroup, carry, new ten, new hundred, place value, algorithm
strings.connection: Days 1–4 made new tens and hundreds in our heads. Today we see them in the standard algorithm.
watchFor: Writing 512 for 27 + 35 (not regrouping): ask "Is it about 60 or about 500?" and show the 12 ones becoming 1 ten and 2 ones.
Carrying without knowing why: ask "What does that little 1 stand for: one, ten, or hundred?"
Preferring a mental strategy: great. Ask them to show where their new ten is in the algorithm.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "In the algorithm, what is the carried 1 really worth?" Land: it is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens), the same thing we did on the number line.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 + 3 + 2, or a known fact. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 12?"
Look for: 27 + 3 + 2. Ask: "Where did the new ten come from?" Model: numberline 27 +3 +2
Look for: 50 + 12, or the algorithm. Ask: "In the algorithm, where is the 12?" Model: column 27 + 35 Model: text 7 + 5 = 12 ones = 1 ten and 2 ones
Look for: the same as 27 + 35, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same in the algorithm?" Model: column 127 + 35
Look for: two regroups (ones and tens). Ask: "How many new tens? How many new hundreds?" Model: column 168 + 57 Model: numberline 168 +32 +25
Look for: the same regroups as 168 + 57, plus 100. Ask: "Predict the answer from the last problem." Model: column 268 + 157
Look for: 400 + 226 - 1 (Day 4!), or the algorithm with three regroups. Ask: "Which way was easier here, and why?" Model: numberline 399 +1 +225, and column 399 + 226

strings.title: Adding Near a Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add a friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: jump, friendly number, back 1, take back.
strings.connection: First string of the routine. Sets up the open number line and jumps.
watchFor: Forgot to take back (48 on problem 3, 58 on problem 4): ask "Is 38 + 9 more or less than 38 + 10?"
Went the wrong way (49 on problem 3): ask the same question and use the line.
Counting up by ones from 38: accept the answer, then ask "Is there a faster jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and where did you land?"
Look for: one jump of 20, or two jumps of 10. Ask: "How is this like the last one?"
Look for: 38 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 38 + 10 help you with 38 + 9?" Word choice: "jump to 48, then back 1".
Look for: 38 + 20, then back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 38 + 9 and 38 + 19?"
Look for: 38 + 30, then back 1. Ask: "Predict what someone will do."
Look for: 38 + 50, then back 1. Ask: "Before I show it, how might someone solve this?"
Look for: 38 + 100, then back 2. Ask: "How is this like problems 3 to 6? What changed?" Word choice: go over the ten (or hundred), then take back the extra.

strings.title: Give and Take
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Move an amount from one number to the other so the total stays the same and one number becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: give, take, move, same total, balance.
strings.connection: Day 1 changed one number and fixed the answer afterwards. Day 2 changes both numbers so the answer never changes.
watchFor: Both numbers moved the same way (50 + 27 for 49 + 26): ask "Did the total stay the same?"
Right amount, only one number changed (50 + 26 = 76): ask "Where did the 1 come from?"
"Add one, take one" with no reason: ask "Why does the total stay the same?" Show two jumps, one growing by 1 and one shrinking by 1.
Students who prefer Day 1's method: accept it, then ask for a second way.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: "same answer as problem 1", or moving 1 from 26 to 49. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why?" Word choice: "give 1 to 49, take 1 from 26".
Look for: moving 2. Ask: "How many does 48 need? Where do they come from?"
Look for: 40 + 35. Ask: "Which number did you make friendly, and why?"
Look for: 60 + 35. Ask: "What changed from problem 4? What happened to the total?"
Look for: 70 + 35. Ask: "How much did you move this time?"
Look for: 200 + 45, or Day 1's way (198 + 50, then back 3). Ask: "Both work. Which is easier here, and why?"

strings.title: Subtraction as Distance
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Subtraction finds the distance between two numbers. Start at the smaller number and add up to the larger.
strings.keywords: distance, difference, gap, how far, add up.
strings.connection: The jumps from Days 1 and 2 now go from the smaller number up to the larger.
watchFor: Borrowing in their heads (21 or 12 for 100 − 89): ask "Where are 89 and 100 on the line?"
10 on problem 3: the 1 from 89 to 90 was left out. Ask "Did you start at 89 or at 90?"
24 on problem 7 (copying the pattern): ask "Are 1002 and 1000 the same number?"
Taking away instead of adding up: accept it, then ask "Which way was the shorter jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "How far is 90 from 100?"
Look for: "98 to 100 is 2" instead of taking away 98. Ask: "Is it easier to take away 98 or to see how far 98 is from 100?"
Look for: 89 to 90 (1), then 90 to 100 (10). Ask: "Where did you stop on the way?"
Look for: 76 to 80 (4), then 80 to 100 (20), or one jump from 76 to 100. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?"
Look for: the same gap as problem 4. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why is it the same?" Word choice: "same gap", "same distance".
Look for: the same gap again. Ask: "Predict 5000 − 4976 before I show it."
Look for: the gap from problem 6, plus 2. Ask: "What changed from problem 6? What happened to the answer?" Word choice: "the top number moved up 2, so the gap grew by 2".

strings.title: Constant Difference
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Sliding both numbers the same amount in the same direction keeps the difference the same. Slide both to make the subtraction friendlier.
strings.keywords: slide, shift, same difference, constant difference.
strings.connection: Day 2 kept the total by moving the numbers in opposite directions. Day 4 keeps the difference by moving both the same way. Day 3, problems 5 and 6 are the first hint.
watchFor: Slid only one number (62 − 50 = 12 for 62 − 49): ask "Did the gap stay the same?" Show both ends moving on the line.
Slid in opposite directions (63 − 48): that is Day 2's move. Ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
"Add 1 to both" with no reason: ask "What happens to the distance between two points if both slide the same way?"
Slid one number, then fixed the answer (62 − 50 = 12, then add 1): this works. Name it as another way.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact.
Look for: the gap is still 4. Ask: "Is this harder than 12 − 8? Why not?"
Look for: 49 to 50 (1), then 50 to 62 (12), or sliding both up 1 to 63 − 50. Ask: "What did you do to make 49 friendlier?"
Look for: the same answer as problem 3. Ask: "What changed from problem 3? What happened to the answer? Why?" Word choice: "I slid both numbers up 1, so the difference stayed the same".
Look for: sliding both up 1 to 163 − 150. Ask: "Predict before I show it."
Look for: the same slide. Ask: "Does the answer depend on how big the numbers are, or how far apart they are?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 73 − 40, or adding up 38 to 40 to 71 (2 + 31). Ask: "Can you slide and add up? Which was quicker?"

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between adding up (distance) and sliding both numbers (same difference), based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: add up, slide, friendly number, efficient, choose.
strings.connection: Combines Days 3 and 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up the slide with Day 2's opposite move: ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"

problems.notes: Look for: adding up. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?"
Look for: adding up from 48, or sliding to 54 − 50.
Look for: 38 to 40 to 70 (2 + 30), or sliding to 72 − 40. Ask: "Which did you choose?"
Look for: sliding to 85 − 40, or adding up 39 to 40 to 84 (1 + 44).
Look for: sliding both up 3 to 606 − 300. Ask: "What made this one easy to slide?"
Look for: adding up 385 to 400 to 1000 (15 + 600), or sliding up 15 to 1015 − 400. Ask: "Why might adding up feel easier here?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 2402 − 2000. Ask: "Which strategy fits this one? How can you tell from the numbers?"

strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: if one number is close to a friendly number, add up or slide, and pick whichever you can do fastest.

strings.title: Times 5 as Half of Times 10
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Multiply by 10 first (easy), then halve to multiply by 5.
strings.keywords: times ten, half, five is half of ten
strings.connection: Week 1 used a friendly number and fixed the answer afterwards. Here the friendly multiplier is 10, and halving fixes it.
watchFor: Halving the wrong number first (18 x 5 as 9 x 5 = 45): ask "Is 18 x 5 about half of 18 x 10, or half of 18?"
Counting by fives or picturing the column method: ask "What would you do for 64 x 5?"
Stuck halving 170 or 340: ask "What is half of 100? Half of 70?" Then add the halves.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does halving 18 x 10 give 18 x 5?" Land: 5 is half of 10, so 5 groups is half of 10 groups.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: half of 80. Ask: "Can 8 x 10 help you with 8 x 5?" Word choice: "half of ten groups is five groups". Model: ratio 1:8, 10:80, 5:40
Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this one too."
Look for: half of 180. Ask: "What is the same as 8 x 5?" Model: ratio 1:18, 10:180, 5:90
Look for: half of 240. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 1:24, 10:240, 5:120
Look for: half of 360. Ask: "Where does the 180 come from?" Model: ratio 1:36, 10:360, 5:180
Look for: half of 170. Ask: "What did you do with the 170?" Word choice: "half of 170 is 85". Model: ratio 1:17, 10:170, 5:85
Look for: half of 640. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 1:64, 10:640, 5:320

strings.title: Double and Halve
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Halve one factor and double the other: the product stays the same and one factor becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: double, halve, same product, friendly number
strings.connection: Day 1 used x10 and halved the answer. Day 2 halves one factor and doubles the other, so the answer never changes (like Week 1, Day 2, Give and Take).
watchFor: Halved both numbers (16 x 25 as 8 x 12.5): ask "Did the product stay the same? What did you do to the 25?"
Doubled both numbers: ask "Is 32 x 50 the same size as 16 x 25?"
A move with no reason ("I just halved it"): ask "Why does the answer stay the same?" Show 4 x 25 as 4 groups of 25, regrouped as 2 groups of 50.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What did you look for in the numbers?" Land: look for a factor you can halve that turns the other factor into a friendly number (25 to 50 to 100).

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact (four quarters). Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: double 100, or 4 x 50. Ask: "What do you notice about 8 x 25 and 4 x 50?" Model: halve 8 x 25 = 4 x 50 = 2 x 100
Look for: 8 x 50, then 4 x 100. Ask: "How many times did you halve? Why stop there?" Model: halve 16 x 25 = 8 x 50 = 4 x 100
Look for: 6 x 50 = 3 x 100, or 3 x 4 x 25. Ask: "What did you do first?" Model: halve 12 x 25 = 6 x 50 = 3 x 100
Look for: 7 x 50, or 10 x 25 + 4 x 25. Ask: "Both work. Which was quicker, and why?" Model: halve 14 x 25 = 7 x 50
Look for: 9 x 100. Ask: "Which number did you halve? What did the 50 become?" Model: halve 18 x 50 = 9 x 100
Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, or 15 x 10 + 15 x 2. Ask: "Which number would you double here, and why?" Model: halve 15 x 12 = 30 x 6

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Multiply by a friendly number just over, then take back the extra groups.
strings.keywords: over, take back, groups, one less group
strings.connection: Week 1, Day 1 went over a ten and took back the extra. Here we go over to a friendly multiplier and take back whole groups.
watchFor: Took back 1, not 1 group (9 x 7 as 70 - 1 = 69): ask "How many sevens are we taking back?"
Used the wrong direction (9 x 7 as 70 + 7): ask "Is 9 x 7 more or less than 10 x 7?"
Counting by nines: accept the answer, then ask "What would you do for 99 x 5?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you take back each time?" Land: one less than a friendly number means one less group, so take back one copy of the other number.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: 70 - 7. Ask: "Can 10 x 7 help you with 9 x 7?" Word choice: "one less group". Model: array 10-1 x 7
Look for: 80 - 8. Ask: "What is the same as 9 x 7?" Model: array 10-1 x 8
Look for: 70 + 7. Ask: "Over or under 10 groups? What do you add?" Model: array 10+1 x 7
Look for: 20 x 8 = 160, then - 8. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: area 20-1 x 8
Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, then - 6. Ask: "Predict what someone will do." Model: area 30-1 x 6
Look for: 50 x 4 = 200, then - 4. Ask: "What is the same about the last three?" Model: area 50-1 x 4
Look for: 100 x 5 = 500, then - 5. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 100-1 x 5

strings.title: Dividing by 5
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Double the dividend, then divide by 10: dividing by 5 gives the same answer as dividing double by double.
strings.keywords: double, divide by ten, same answer, how many fives
strings.connection: Day 1 halved to multiply by 5. Day 4 does the opposite: double, then divide by 10. Both use 10 as the friendly number.
watchFor: Halved instead of doubled (80 / 5 as 40 / 10 = 4): ask "Is 80 / 5 less than 80 / 10?"
Divided by 10 and stopped (80 / 5 = 8): ask "How many fives fit in 80? Is it as many as tens?"
Divided by 10 first, then doubled (135 / 10 = 13.5, then 27): accept it, name it as another way, and check the 13.5 jump.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does doubling both numbers keep the answer the same?" Land: 80 / 5 and 160 / 10 ask the same question, how many fives fit, so the answer stays the same.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: double 8, or 160 / 10. Ask: "Why is it more than 80 / 10?" Word choice: "twice as many fives as tens". Model: ratio 80:5, 160:10, 16:1
Look for: 70 / 10. Ask: "What did you do to 35?" Model: ratio 35:5, 70:10, 7:1
Look for: 150 / 10. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 75:5, 150:10, 15:1
Look for: 270 / 10. Ask: "How did you double 135?" Word choice: "double the hundred, double the thirty-five". Model: ratio 135:5, 270:10, 27:1
Look for: 480 / 10. Ask: "Is this the same move as Day 1 turned around?" Model: ratio 240:5, 480:10, 48:1
Look for: 840 / 10. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 420:5, 840:10, 84:1

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between half of x10, double and halve, over and back, and double then divide by 10, based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: choose, friendly number, halve, double, over and back
strings.connection: Combines Days 1 to 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up directions (halving to divide by 5, doubling to multiply by 5): ask "Does the answer get bigger or smaller?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: look for 5, 25, 50 (halve or double), a number just under a friendly number (over and back), or a division by 5 (double).

problems.notes: Look for: half of 260. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?" Model: text 26 x 10 = 260 ; half is 130
Look for: 12 x 100, or 24 x 50 = 12 x 100. Ask: "What made 25 easy to work with?" Model: text 48 x 25 = 24 x 50 ; = 12 x 100
Look for: 140 - 14. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: text 10 x 14 = 140 ; 140 - 14 = 126
Look for: 390 / 10. Ask: "Which Day 4 move did you use?" Model: text 195 / 5 = 390 / 10 ; = 39
Look for: 240 - 8. Ask: "What made this one easy to adjust?" Model: text 30 x 8 = 240 ; 240 - 8 = 232
Look for: 500 - 10, or half of 980. Ask: "Two good ways. Which feels quicker, and why?" Model: text 100 x 5 = 500 ; 500 - 10 = 490
Look for: 8 x 70, or 4 x 140, or 16 x 30 + 16 x 5. Ask: "Which number did you halve?" Model: halve 16 x 35 = 8 x 70 = 4 x 140
